title: Deduplication
summary_md: Remove or find repeated rows: DISTINCT vs GROUP BY, duplicate detection, cleaned comparison keys, one-row-per-key with ROW_NUMBER, and safe deletes.

sections.heading: DISTINCT vs GROUP BY
sections.body_md:
- `SELECT DISTINCT a, b` removes duplicate **whole output rows**; it is not a function of one column.
- `GROUP BY a, b` returns the same unique combinations, and lets you add aggregates (`COUNT(*)`, `MIN`, `MAX`).
- Both treat **NULLs as equal** to each other (one NULL group), unlike `=`.
- `COUNT(*)` counts rows, `COUNT(col)` skips NULLs, `COUNT(DISTINCT col)` counts unique non-NULL values.

syntax.mysql:
SELECT DISTINCT col1, col2 FROM t;
SELECT col1, col2, COUNT(*) FROM t GROUP BY col1, col2;
syntax.tsql:
SELECT DISTINCT col1, col2 FROM t;
SELECT col1, col2, COUNT(*) FROM t GROUP BY col1, col2;

args.name: DISTINCT
args.meaning: Applies to the entire select list, not just the first column. `DISTINCT(a), b` is the same as `DISTINCT a, b`.

args.name: GROUP BY cols
args.meaning: Defines the uniqueness key; every non-aggregated select column must be listed.

examples.title: Distinct cities
examples.explain_md: Three Austin accounts collapse to one row, and the NULL city survives as a single row (NULLs sort first).

examples.title: DISTINCT applies to the whole row
examples.explain_md: Customer 2 placed two orders on 2024-02-03; the pair `(customer_id, order_date)` appears once, giving 13 rows from 14 orders.

examples.title: GROUP BY gives the same combinations plus counts
examples.explain_md: For customer 2, the 02-03 group has 2 rows totalling 75.00.
examples.mysql:
SELECT customer_id, order_date, COUNT(*) AS n_rows, SUM(amount) AS total
FROM orders
WHERE customer_id = 2
GROUP BY customer_id, order_date
ORDER BY order_date;
examples.tsql:
SELECT customer_id, order_date, COUNT(*) AS n_rows, SUM(amount) AS total
FROM orders
WHERE customer_id = 2
GROUP BY customer_id, order_date
ORDER BY order_date;

examples.title: COUNT(*) vs COUNT(col) vs COUNT(DISTINCT col)
examples.explain_md: Six accounts, five with a city, three distinct cities.
examples.mysql:
SELECT COUNT(*) AS total_rows,
       COUNT(city) AS non_null_city,
       COUNT(DISTINCT city) AS distinct_city
FROM customers;
examples.tsql:
SELECT COUNT(*) AS total_rows,
       COUNT(city) AS non_null_city,
       COUNT(DISTINCT city) AS distinct_city
FROM customers;

pitfalls_md: `SELECT DISTINCT` on a wide table hides the real problem (which key is duplicated?). Find duplicates by key first, then decide.

sections.heading: Finding duplicates
sections.body_md:
- Decide the **business key** (what makes two rows 'the same'), group by it, and keep groups with `HAVING COUNT(*) > 1`.
- To see the actual rows, use a window count (`COUNT(*) OVER (PARTITION BY key)`) and filter in an outer query, or join back to the duplicate keys.
- `HAVING` filters groups after aggregation; `WHERE` filters rows before.

syntax.mysql: SELECT key_cols, COUNT(*) FROM t GROUP BY key_cols HAVING COUNT(*) > 1;
syntax.tsql: SELECT key_cols, COUNT(*) FROM t GROUP BY key_cols HAVING COUNT(*) > 1;

args.name: HAVING COUNT(*) > 1
args.meaning: Keeps only keys that occur more than once.

examples.title: Duplicate keys
examples.mysql:
SELECT customer_id, order_date, COUNT(*) AS n
FROM orders
GROUP BY customer_id, order_date
HAVING COUNT(*) > 1
ORDER BY customer_id, order_date;
examples.tsql:
SELECT customer_id, order_date, COUNT(*) AS n
FROM orders
GROUP BY customer_id, order_date
HAVING COUNT(*) > 1
ORDER BY customer_id, order_date;

examples.title: Show the duplicate rows themselves
examples.explain_md: A window count tags every row with its group size, so the full rows (orders 104 and 105) come back.
examples.mysql:
SELECT order_id, customer_id, order_date, amount
FROM (SELECT order_id, customer_id, order_date, amount,
             COUNT(*) OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id, order_date) AS n
      FROM orders) AS x
WHERE n > 1
ORDER BY order_id;
examples.tsql:
SELECT order_id, customer_id, order_date, amount
FROM (SELECT order_id, customer_id, order_date, amount,
             COUNT(*) OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id, order_date) AS n
      FROM orders) AS x
WHERE n > 1
ORDER BY order_id;

examples.title: How many surplus rows?
examples.explain_md: Surplus = rows beyond the first in each group. `SUM(n - 1)` is how many a dedup would remove.
examples.mysql:
SELECT SUM(n - 1) AS surplus_rows
FROM (SELECT COUNT(*) AS n
      FROM orders
      GROUP BY customer_id, order_date) AS g;
examples.tsql:
SELECT SUM(n - 1) AS surplus_rows
FROM (SELECT COUNT(*) AS n
      FROM orders
      GROUP BY customer_id, order_date) AS g;

sections.heading: Normalising before comparing
sections.body_md:
- Real duplicates differ by case, padding or formatting. Compare a **cleaned key**: `LOWER(TRIM(col))`.
- Use the same expression in `GROUP BY` / `PARTITION BY` and in the select list.
- Comparison rules depend on collation: both engines default to case-insensitive, but trailing-space handling differs (MySQL 8 default compares trailing spaces; SQL Server ignores them). Normalise explicitly instead of relying on it.
- `GROUP BY` / `DISTINCT` treat NULL as one value; joins on `=` do not match NULL to NULL (MySQL `<=>`, SQL Server 2022 `IS NOT DISTINCT FROM`).

syntax.tsql: LOWER(LTRIM(RTRIM(email)))   -- TRIM(email) also works on SQL Server 2017+

args.name: TRIM(x)
args.meaning: Removes leading and trailing spaces (MySQL: also `TRIM(BOTH ch FROM x)`).

args.name: LOWER(x)
args.meaning: Lower-cases so 'PABLO@' and 'pablo@' match regardless of collation.

examples.title: Compute the key
examples.explain_md: Customers 4 and 6 differ only by case and a trailing space; their cleaned keys are identical.

examples.title: Duplicate groups on the cleaned key
examples.explain_md: One group has two accounts: keep 4 (earliest id), consider 6 the duplicate.
examples.mysql:
SELECT LOWER(TRIM(email)) AS email_key,
       COUNT(*) AS n,
       MIN(customer_id) AS keep_id,
       MAX(customer_id) AS latest_id
FROM customers
GROUP BY LOWER(TRIM(email))
HAVING COUNT(*) > 1
ORDER BY email_key;
examples.tsql:
SELECT LOWER(TRIM(email)) AS email_key,
       COUNT(*) AS n,
       MIN(customer_id) AS keep_id,
       MAX(customer_id) AS latest_id
FROM customers
GROUP BY LOWER(TRIM(email))
HAVING COUNT(*) > 1
ORDER BY email_key;

pitfalls_md: Stripping inner whitespace needs `REPLACE(col, ' ', '')`; TRIM only touches the ends.
Normalising in the comparison defeats an index on `email`; for big tables store the cleaned key as a computed column.

sections.heading: Latest or first row per key with ROW_NUMBER
sections.body_md:
- Number the rows inside each key and keep `rn = 1`: `ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY key ORDER BY ...)`.
- **Keep-last** = order by the timestamp `DESC`; **keep-first** = order `ASC`.
- Always add a **deterministic tie-breaker** (a unique id) as the last ORDER BY column; without it, ties pick an arbitrary row that can change between runs.
- `RANK` / `DENSE_RANK` keep ties and so cannot deduplicate on their own.
- If you only need aggregate columns, `GROUP BY key` with `MAX()` is simpler.

syntax.mysql: ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY key ORDER BY pref_col DESC, unique_id DESC)
syntax.tsql: ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY key ORDER BY pref_col DESC, unique_id DESC)

args.name: PARTITION BY key
args.meaning: The business key; one survivor per partition.

args.name: ORDER BY pref_col
args.meaning: Which row survives: DESC for newest, ASC for oldest.

args.name: unique_id
args.meaning: Tie-breaker. Without it, equal `pref_col` values give a non-deterministic winner.

examples.title: Latest order per customer
examples.explain_md: Descending date, then descending `order_id` as the tie-breaker.
examples.mysql:
WITH numbered AS (
  SELECT order_id, customer_id, order_date, amount,
         ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id
                            ORDER BY order_date DESC, order_id DESC) AS rn
  FROM orders
)
SELECT order_id, customer_id, order_date, amount
FROM numbered
WHERE rn = 1
ORDER BY customer_id;
examples.tsql:
WITH numbered AS (
  SELECT order_id, customer_id, order_date, amount,
         ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id
                            ORDER BY order_date DESC, order_id DESC) AS rn
  FROM orders
)
SELECT order_id, customer_id, order_date, amount
FROM numbered
WHERE rn = 1
ORDER BY customer_id;

examples.title: One top earner per department
examples.explain_md: Ben and Cara tie at 150000; `emp_id` in the ORDER BY makes Ben win every time, so Engineering returns one row.
examples.mysql:
WITH numbered AS (
  SELECT dept, name, salary,
         ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY dept ORDER BY salary DESC, emp_id) AS rn
  FROM employees
)
SELECT dept, name, salary
FROM numbered
WHERE rn = 1
ORDER BY dept;
examples.tsql:
WITH numbered AS (
  SELECT dept, name, salary,
         ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY dept ORDER BY salary DESC, emp_id) AS rn
  FROM employees
)
SELECT dept, name, salary
FROM numbered
WHERE rn = 1
ORDER BY dept;

examples.title: Keep-first vs keep-last on the cleaned email
examples.explain_md: Two numberings side by side: account 4 is first and 6 is last in the pablo group; everyone else is both.
examples.mysql:
WITH k AS (
  SELECT customer_id, name, signup_date,
         ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY LOWER(TRIM(email))
                            ORDER BY signup_date, customer_id) AS rn_first,
         ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY LOWER(TRIM(email))
                            ORDER BY signup_date DESC, customer_id DESC) AS rn_last
  FROM customers
)
SELECT customer_id, name, rn_first, rn_last
FROM k
ORDER BY customer_id;
examples.tsql:
WITH k AS (
  SELECT customer_id, name, signup_date,
         ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY LOWER(TRIM(email))
                            ORDER BY signup_date, customer_id) AS rn_first,
         ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY LOWER(TRIM(email))
                            ORDER BY signup_date DESC, customer_id DESC) AS rn_last
  FROM customers
)
SELECT customer_id, name, rn_first, rn_last
FROM k
ORDER BY customer_id;

examples.title: The deduplicated customer list (keep first)
examples.explain_md: Filtering on `rn_first = 1` drops the later duplicate (account 6).
examples.mysql:
WITH k AS (
  SELECT customer_id, name, email, signup_date,
         ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY LOWER(TRIM(email))
                            ORDER BY signup_date, customer_id) AS rn
  FROM customers
)
SELECT customer_id, name, email, signup_date
FROM k
WHERE rn = 1
ORDER BY customer_id;
examples.tsql:
WITH k AS (
  SELECT customer_id, name, email, signup_date,
         ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY LOWER(TRIM(email))
                            ORDER BY signup_date, customer_id) AS rn
  FROM customers
)
SELECT customer_id, name, email, signup_date
FROM k
WHERE rn = 1
ORDER BY customer_id;

examples.title: When only aggregates are needed: GROUP BY + MAX
examples.explain_md: No window needed for 'last order date per customer'; use ROW_NUMBER only when you need the other columns of that row.
examples.mysql:
SELECT customer_id, MAX(order_date) AS last_order_date
FROM orders
GROUP BY customer_id
ORDER BY customer_id;
examples.tsql:
SELECT customer_id, MAX(order_date) AS last_order_date
FROM orders
GROUP BY customer_id
ORDER BY customer_id;

pitfalls_md: No tie-breaker: re-running the query (or the DELETE) can keep a different row each time.

sections.heading: Deleting duplicates
sections.body_md:
- **Always preview first**: run the SELECT that lists the rows with `rn > 1`, check the count, then delete.
- **MySQL**: cannot select from the table being deleted in a subquery directly (error 1093), so wrap the numbered rows in a derived table. `DELETE ... WHERE id IN (SELECT id FROM (...) AS d WHERE rn > 1)`.
- **SQL Server**: delete straight through a CTE; the rows are removed from the underlying table. `WITH d AS (SELECT ..., ROW_NUMBER() ...) DELETE FROM d WHERE rn > 1;`
- Do it inside a transaction, and add a `UNIQUE` constraint afterwards so duplicates cannot return.
- Huge tables: build a clean copy (`CREATE TABLE ... AS SELECT` / `SELECT INTO`) and swap names rather than deleting millions of rows.
- The examples below are the previews (SELECTs) of what each DELETE would remove.

syntax.tsql:
WITH d AS (
  SELECT customer_id,
         ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY LOWER(TRIM(email))
                            ORDER BY signup_date, customer_id) AS rn
  FROM customers
)
DELETE FROM d WHERE rn > 1;

args.name: derived table d
args.meaning: MySQL: forces the numbering to be materialised so the DELETE target is not read live (avoids error 1093).

args.name: DELETE FROM d
args.meaning: SQL Server: deleting from a CTE that selects one base table deletes from that table.

args.name: rn > 1
args.meaning: Everything except the survivor of each partition.

examples.title: Preview: duplicate customers to delete (keep first)
examples.explain_md: Only account 6 would be deleted. In MySQL the numbering lives in a derived table, in SQL Server in a CTE; both are the exact shape the DELETE uses.
examples.mysql:
SELECT d.customer_id, d.name, d.email
FROM (SELECT customer_id, name, email,
             ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY LOWER(TRIM(email))
                                ORDER BY signup_date, customer_id) AS rn
      FROM customers) AS d
WHERE d.rn > 1
ORDER BY d.customer_id;
examples.tsql:
WITH d AS (
  SELECT customer_id, name, email,
         ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY LOWER(TRIM(email))
                            ORDER BY signup_date, customer_id) AS rn
  FROM customers
)
SELECT customer_id, name, email
FROM d
WHERE rn > 1
ORDER BY customer_id;

examples.title: Preview: duplicate orders (same customer and day)
examples.explain_md: Keeping the lowest `order_id` per customer-day means order 105 is the surplus row.
examples.mysql:
SELECT d.order_id, d.customer_id, d.order_date, d.amount
FROM (SELECT order_id, customer_id, order_date, amount,
             ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id, order_date ORDER BY order_id) AS rn
      FROM orders) AS d
WHERE d.rn > 1
ORDER BY d.order_id;
examples.tsql:
WITH d AS (
  SELECT order_id, customer_id, order_date, amount,
         ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id, order_date ORDER BY order_id) AS rn
  FROM orders
)
SELECT order_id, customer_id, order_date, amount
FROM d
WHERE rn > 1
ORDER BY order_id;

examples.title: Verify: rows now vs unique keys
examples.explain_md: Before the delete: 6 rows but 5 unique cleaned emails. After a correct delete both numbers are 5.

pitfalls_md: Run the preview SELECT and compare the count to your surplus-row count before any DELETE.
Dedup rules (what is 'the same', which row survives) are a business decision: state your assumption in the interview.
